theme: My God, my God, the psalm Hebrews draws from
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 22 slowly, in two sittings if needed. The first twenty-one verses are a cry of anguish, and the last ten are a shout of praise. The psalm is quoted or alluded to by Hebrews, Matthew, Mark, John, and Paul. As you read, think of Jesus on the cross, because his own words from the cross are the opening line.
settingTheScene: Psalm 22 is one of the most important psalms in the Bible and one of the most poignant. David wrote it, but he writes with details that go beyond anything that happened to him. As you read, you will find a description of crucifixion centuries before it was invented. Jesus quoted the first line while hanging on the cross, and the Gospel writers echo it in the details they record. The author of Hebrews also draws from this psalm. In Hebrews 2:12, the Son says to the Father, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise,” quoting Psalm 22:22. We close the unit with this psalm because it shows the cost of the salvation Hebrews has described and the triumph that follows.
observation: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (v. 1). Jesus quoted this on the cross (Matthew 27:46).
David trusts that God is holy and was faithful to the fathers who cried out and were delivered (vv. 3-5).
“But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people” (v. 6).
Mockers say, “He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him” (v. 8), the same words the leaders used at the cross (Matthew 27:43).
“They have pierced my hands and feet” (v. 16). The bones are out of joint, the tongue sticks to the jaws, and they divide his garments by lot (vv. 14-18).
At verse 22, the psalm turns: “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you.”
God “has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted” (v. 24).
The psalm ends with the whole earth turning to the LORD and a people yet unborn hearing “that he has done it” (vv. 27-31).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with the cry of a person who feels abandoned by God. “Why have you forsaken me?” The question is honest, and the psalm does not rush to resolve it. David describes the experience of suffering with God’s apparent silence. He cries day and night, and there is no answer.

Yet even in the dark, David does not let go of God. “Yet you are holy” (v. 3). The word “yet” is the hinge of the first section. His present experience says God has left, but his history says God does not abandon those who trust him. The fathers cried and were delivered. So he continues to cry.

Verses 6-21 are a vivid, almost cinematic description of suffering. David describes himself as a worm, scorned and mocked. People gather like bulls and lions and dogs. His strength is poured out like water, his heart melts like wax, and his tongue sticks to his jaws. They have pierced his hands and feet. They divide his garments. No known event in David’s life matches these details. They fit the crucifixion exactly. Christ on the cross experienced what David described: the mockery, the thirst, the pierced hands, and the soldiers casting lots for his clothing. The psalm is a Spirit-given portrait of the Messiah’s sufferings, and it was written about a thousand years before they happened.

When Jesus cried “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”, he was not only expressing pain. He was identifying with the entire psalm. He took on himself the experience of being forsaken so that we never will be. The wrath that should have fallen on us fell on him, and in that moment he experienced the separation from the Father that sin deserves. This is the mystery of the atonement, and it is the reason the author of Hebrews can say that Christ’s sacrifice is enough.

Then the psalm turns in verse 22, and the tone changes entirely. The sufferer is rescued. “You have answered me.” And now he promises to declare God’s name to his brothers and praise him in the congregation. This is the resurrection, which is the Father’s answer to the cry. Hebrews 2:12 puts these words in the mouth of the risen Christ, who stands among his people and leads their worship. And the effect reaches to the ends of the earth. “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD.” A people yet unborn, including us, will be told of what he has done. The final word of the psalm is that “he has done it.” This is the Hebrew equivalent of “It is finished.”
connection: Psalm 22 is quoted or echoed throughout the crucifixion narratives: Matthew 27:35-46, Mark 15:24-34, Luke 23:34, and John 19:23-24. Hebrews 2:12 quotes verse 22. The suffering servant of Isaiah 53 parallels this psalm. The final verses link to the Abrahamic promise of blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:3) and to the Great Commission in Matthew 28.
application:
First, let this psalm give you language for your own darkest moments. If you have ever felt abandoned by God, you are not the first. The psalm models honest crying out and a refusal to let go of God’s character.

Second, consider what Jesus did for you. He was forsaken so that you will never be. When you feel alone, remember that your Savior has been there and has made a way for you to be accepted.

Third, take the praise section seriously. David vows to tell others of God’s deliverance. Who could you tell this week about what Christ has done?

Fourth, spend some time in silent gratitude. The one who suffered this was your substitute.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being forsaken in your place.
Thank God that he did not hide his face.
Praise him for the great congregation.
